item.title: To baldly go: Patrick Stewart was an icon for bald men everywhere
item.description: The actor was an exemplary bald star, embracing his hair loss and the freedoms it brought. He didn’t go grey or recede – and he didn’t wear a wig like William Shatner as Captain Kirk Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86 Patrick Stewart managed to be lots of different things at once. He was a towering figure on stage. He was a literal superhero onscreen. And, at times, he wasn’t above sending himself up. It also needs to be said that he was a bald man. And a pioneering one at that. Nowhere was this more clear than during his stint on Star Trek: The Next Generation. Previously, Star Trek had been a kind of space-set action show, where the relentlessly virile Captain Kirk would beam down to new planets to either punch or get off with all the aliens there. But then came its successor, and Kirk was replaced by a nonviolent intellectual called Jean-Luc. Worse still, he didn’t have any hair. What a sign of weakness. Continue reading...

Mini and Miki (the Disney mouse names in Serbian) are a sometime boyfriend and girlfriend living in Austria. item.title: Forget water features – a tiny pond will bring wildlife to your garden
item.description: You might think ponds are complicated things with liners, but you can make one from a washing-up bowl Do you remember the 90s, when everyone was obsessed with “water features”, mostly thanks to Charlie Dimmock? A simpler time. Perhaps I’m hanging out with the wrong garden designers, but I rarely hear much talk of water features now. For years, Chelsea flower show gardens have featured subtle Cor-Ten steel-clad trickles or elegant mirrored ponds. There have been a fair few naturalistic streams (such as A Rewilding Britain Landscape by Lulu Urquhart and Adam Hunt, with beaver-gnawed twigs, which controversially won best in show in 2022), but scant fountains or burbling rocks. Water features are out, I guess. Ponds are in. My mum built one the other day. Hers is smaller than a piece of A3, lined with rocks and terracotta seedling pots, with two metal ducks stuck around the edge in a boggy bit of her compact urban garden. Many government critics say they still fear abduction, arbitrary arrest and politically motivated prosecutions.

item.title: ‘Swift justice’: Student List supporters focus on cleaning up Serbia’s rotten institutions

One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees. That’s perhaps the most commonplace horror of our times, whether on the internet or politics, and you feel the tremors of it steadily breaking the surface in Yoo Ah-in’s performance. He plays Jong-su, an aspiring writer, quietly frustrated with his lot in life. Jong-su works odd jobs and tends to his incarcerated father’s dilapidated farm, growing more desperate to grasp some sense of control over the world around him, which is where the scary part comes in. item.title: Radie Peat: No Human Tongue Can Tell review – Lankum singer’s solo debut is the year’s best folk album
item.description: (Rough Trade) Collecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering power Lankum singer Radie Peat’s extraordinary debut album begins without frills or ornament: just her voice, stark and low, each breath like air vibrating through the metal reeds of a harmonium. Singing Hares on the Mountain to the tune Shirley Collins arranged for 1964’s Folk Roots, New Routes, Peat accompanies herself subtly on Fender Rhodes piano before adding layers of Mellotron and Wurlitzer. Her simple, quiet approach is consistently startling and profoundly moving. No Human Tongue Can Tell collects songs of female struggle, suffering, strength and endurance, although Peat only realised this, she writes in her liner notes, after limiting her choices by her “own mind and abilities” and “personal preferences”. item.title: Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo review – a slippery liar’s tale
item.description: Shortlisted for the Goldsmiths prize, this compelling interrogation of memory, justice and truth offers no easy answers The Goldsmiths prize-shortlisted debut from British-Greek author Aea Varfis-van Warmelo opens with a confession: “I have never told this story before.” The narrator, who bears the author’s name, goes on to tell the reader that she is a liar. From Humbert Humbert’s self-justifying account of abuse in Lolita to the devastating misinterpretation at the heart of Ian McEwan’s Atonement, the trope of the unreliable narrator exposes the dangerous gap between the stories we tell and the truths they obscure. In Attention Seeking Behaviour, the reader is asked to examine their own capacity for trust. A young woman aspires to be a writer – yet she has paused her postgraduate degree in poetry. She works unfulfilling jobs that demand little from her and has a lot of sex, which she describes as offering her “solitude”. She does all this while lying compulsively. She lies for fun, t

item.title: ‘Expect goosebumps!’: to celebrate Halloween, readers choose the spookiest places in the UK
item.description: From a ghostly hill fort on the South Downs to a haunted farmhouse in remote Northern Ireland, you guide us to some frightfully scary places • Tell us about an escape in the wilds of Scotland – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher Dunnottar Castle , perched on cliffs above the crashing North Sea, is one of Scotland’s eeriest places. The most haunting part is the Whigs Vault, where more than 160 prisoners were confined in dreadful conditions in 1685. Standing in that dark chamber, it’s impossible not to imagine their fear and suffering. With my Fraser ancestry, the castle’s history feels especially poignant. The names of multiple Frasers are recorded, their details written on the wall. The wind whistles through the stonework, the waves thunder below, and there’s a sense that the past hasn’t quite left. It’s beautiful, tragic and wonderfully spooky, especially beneath Aberdeenshire’s brooding grey skies. Rosie Continue reading...

item.title: Biodiversity Cop17 seems to be stalling. Is it time to reform the process?
item.description: In this week’s newsletter: There are too many meetings, and not enough decisions, say experts – and time is running out • Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here When things are not going well at an environmental summit, organisers often tell delegates that the “world is watching” in an attempt to focus minds. But spend any time at biodiversity Cop17 in Armenia and it is clear that the world’s attention is elsewhere. The negotiating halls of Yerevan’s Meridian centre are subdued. Environment ministers have arrived from all corners of the world to plan their response to being so far behind the biodiversity targets they agreed four years ago. Right now, they appear on track to miss nearly all of them. They risk continuing the miserable record of never having met a biodiversity target they have set for themselves. item.title: Opening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon Jenkins
item.description: Andy Burnham must tread cautiously, but Brexit was a very grave act of self-harm – and he is right to address it Andy Burnham’s opening debate on whether Britain should rejoin the EU is divisive, painful and politically risky. That is why it should be welcomed. To jeopardise his popularity so soon after coming to office might seem reckless, but the issue is urgent and not going away. Brexit is continuing to damage the nation’s economy. The prime minister’s job is to challenge, if not reform it. The Brexit decade has evoked a bizarre sense of guilt among Britons. Opinion polls show nearly 60% regard it as a mistake, with just a third still in favour. Almost a quarter of those who voted for Brexit now regret it. While early forecasts of economic disaster were proved wrong , the accumulated cost of cutting links with Britain’s biggest trading partner is estimated at 6-8% of GDP . item.title: Country diary: The light and shade of autumn’s shortening days | Merryn Glover
item.description: Loch Insh, Cairngorms: In my three decades in Scotland I’ve adjusted to the darkness of this time of year, and found glory in the quality of light It is the one clear day in a fortnight of heavy cloud, wind and rain, so I am out by the loch, basking in the rays of light, breathing them in, hoarding for the weeks to come. This time of year makes them all the more precious. Here in the Highlands, once we are past the autumnal equinox , we can almost feel the Earth tipping away from the sun as the light grows shorter each day and the night steals back. item.title: Experience: I live in the house from the 80s horror movie Poltergeist
item.description: I was a fan of the film, so when it came on the market, I snapped it up. Now I allow other fans to come and stay in this piece of Hollywood history I first saw Poltergeist at the movie theatre with my mom and sisters, back when it came out in 1982. I remember being scared, especially during the part when the toy clown drags little Robbie Freeling under the bed. At that age, the idea of a family experiencing something terrifying in the kind of everyday suburban house I was familiar with made a big impression. Later, it became a ritual of mine to put the movie on every Halloween. I grew up in the Chicago area, but moved to California in the early 90s to go to art college. My sister moved there, too – to Simi Valley, not far from the house used as the Freeling family’s home in the movie. I’d drive past it when I visited her. item.title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
item.description: As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.” The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit. That perhaps explains the Broadway revival of A Few Good Men, Aaron Sorkin’s 1989 courtroom drama about a cocky military attorney defending two young marines who followed an illegal order with fatal results. The play is at once sharp and misty-eyed, critiquing a hallowed institution while reverently imbuing it with a certain dignity – in some ways, it does for the military what Sorkin’s The West Wing did for the Oval Office. item.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
item.description: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.

item.title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
item.description: The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France. The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world. item.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
item.description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them. And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings. item.title: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine
item.description: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys It’s early 1998, and at Fort Apache recording studio in Massachusetts, Mark Sandman, the suave frontman of Morphine, is nearing breaking point. Morphine’s four enigmatic and blackly humorous albums have won critical acclaim and, lately, unexpected commercial success considering their uncompromising creative vision. After the excesses of grunge, Sandman considered their idiosyncratic blend of sophisticated storytelling, prowling slide-bass and Dana Colley’s atmospheric saxophone a kind of “palate cleanser”. In 1997 Morphine had signed to DreamWorks Records, founded by industry bigwigs David Geffen and Mo Ostin. item.title: My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do? | Leading questions
item.description: A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in reality Read more Leading questions My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. No matter how high or low the stakes, she has to win. When she doesn’t, she becomes explosive with rage, and often upends the game, sweeps dice off the table, or storms off in a rage. She is otherwise a normal and lovely person, with whom I get on very well. Seeing this side of her makes me deeply uncomfortable and it feels really childish and inappropriate. Will she behave that way with me if I say or do something she doesn’t like? I think in an effort to smooth the tension, my husband’s family always laughs and teases her about her reaction. The results are joyfully convincing From the outside, it looks as if things have gone swimmingly for the Big Moon. Fronted by Juliette Jackson, a former waitress who dreamed big, they have been active for 12 years, a success in itself in these days, notching up four albums including this latest. Delve beneath the surface, however, and things haven’t always been so sunny. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. item.title: Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – a novelist unleashed
item.description: The constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacy Some months after returning home, after a grim year in hospitals in Rome and London, Hanif Kureishi begins to rebel. Not against his family, or the physical reality of being tetraplegic (and how could he?), but the liberal homogeneity of Shepherd’s Bush. He gets a diamond stud in his left ear at Westfield shopping centre, a piercing that enraged his father when he was 17. He sends off for a Maga cap and wears both to the farmers’ market, hoping for vitriol but getting nothing. “These quiescent scumbags only cared about themselves and their shopping,” he grumbles. “Being a fascist is far less thrilling than I imagined.” Kureishi’s “re-punking” after decades in the metropolitan elite remains an ongoing project, just one response to his paralysis after a fall on Boxing Day 2022. item.title: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe
item.description: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in Senegal About 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano. The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at th

item.title: Football Daily | Fleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dream
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! item.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: to nail this year’s British heritage look, just study Rivals
item.description: Thanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right now British heritage, in fashion terms, is a country where it is permanently October. A conker-brown and pleasant land, if you will. Brand Britain in the style sense comes into its own in autumn: roaring fires, muddy lanes, damp dogs. Waxed jackets and chunky knits, tartan and tweed, jaunty scarves to banish draughts. Clothes for going on a hearty walk, but with a hip flask in your pocket. Fashion has been mining this seam since long before Brideshead Revisited made battered evening dresses and Oxford bags look romantic, and it keeps returning, because trad British style is satisfyingly utilitarian while also being loaded with enough backstory (class, history, eccentricity) to be intriguing and reinventable. item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11335-4 Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination

item.title: Why did ancient humans avoid this lush paradise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03486-1 A new expedition into the Rub’ al Khali desert finds no evidence of ancient human settlement.

item.title: This Arabian desert was once a lush paradise. Why did ancient humans avoid it?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03484-3 Expedition revealed that water wasn’t enough for human settlement — plus, proposals to block sunlight get serious.

item.title: Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03260-3 A map of Africa’s water demand reveals that the scarcity of water is only part of the problem facing the continent — management is a separate challenge.

item.title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03444-x Faulty neurons can contribute to various neurological conditions, but researchers have uncovered a system that might clean them up.

item.title: Daily briefing: The big push to personalize psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03531-z A data-driven approach could match treatments to individuals with more precision. Plus, funders in Europe are backing preprint-led publishing and whether professors should care about student evaluations.

item.title: Tethered to stone: how rock and water availability shaped early desert occupation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03263-0 Fresh water in deserts often points to sites with signs of early humans and stone tools. But, in Arabia’s Rub’ al Khali region, water alone does not predict occupation.

item.title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02202-3 A jury weighs in on whether teaching assessments are popularity contests or an important tool.

item.title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03402-7 Fresh ideas are welcome in a discipline in which progress is rare — provided they are applied rigorously.

item.title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03261-2 A cellular fuel called lactate is channelled directly into energy-generating organelles in heart muscle, defying the prevailing view about lactate transport.

item.title: Clues about complex life come from freshly cultivated archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03294-7 Two archaeal strains that belong to a lineage closely related to the ancestor of eukaryotic cells (complex cells with membrane-bound organelles) have been brought into culture. Their simple internal organization, elaborate surface structures, microbial partnerships and protein-dependent lifestyle provide clues about how eukaryotic cells arose.

item.title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03445-w European funders put weight behind emerging ‘publish, review, curate’ approach for preprints.

item.title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03325-3 As poor publishing practices proliferate, scholarly databases are under pressure to ensure the titles they list are reputable.

item.title: Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03476-3 A marked rise in submissions for the European Research Council’s grants is pushing down success rates.

item.title: Dengue comes back even in vaccinated people — new clues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03488-z Researchers help to answer a question dogging the development of improved vaccines against the mosquito-borne disease.

item.title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03391-7 Could a blood sample, a brain scan and a look at your phone data transform how your psychiatrist treats you?

item.title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03415-2 Some say the concept is complete fantasy, but a detailed analysis suggests that the falling cost of rocket launches might make it feasible in a few decades.

item.title: An unexpected function of a cell-cycle enzyme might explain the toxic effects of its inhibitors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03288-5 A previously unknown mechanism required for cells to start proliferating has been identified. A combination of mathematical modelling and cell-based experiments shows that the enzyme WEE1 switches off a protein-degradation complex to allow cell proliferation to start, with implications for WEE1 inhibitors currently in trials for cancer treatments.

item.title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03262-1 A first-of-its kind consortium reveals a lack of correlation between behavioural and neural measures of a person’s emotional regulation.

item.title: How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03248-z The largest analysis of its kind reveals the public’s changing relationship with science and the people who do it.

item.title: Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03067-2 Single-cell profiling of nearly 2,000 people brings scientists closer to understanding the link between genetic variation, gene expression and health.

item.title: Ribbon made of carbon pentagons and heptagons has metallic properties
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03298-3 Ribbons that are composed exclusively of five- and seven-carbon rings have metal-like electron transport and conductance. The ribbons can be synthesized by linking previously inaccessible chains of paired five-membered rings, providing a route to making highly conducting carbon nanoribbons.

item.title: Where have all the saucers flown?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03107-x Missed encounters.

item.title: The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02670-7 A project to improve understanding of an often-neglected group in academia aims to help its members to navigate career uncertainty.

item.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11180-5 A geoarchaeological survey of the Rub’ al Khali (the Empty Quarter of Arabia) and spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula suggest that human settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and stone suitable for making tools, rather than water alone.

item.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11211-1 A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

item.title: Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10438-2 Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

item.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11223-x Pseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.

item.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11190-3 Single-neuron sequencing shows that widespread genomic abnormalities are common prenatally but largely eliminated around birth, indicating developmental genome quality control in human neurons.

item.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11195-y Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

item.title: Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11202-2 Planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons are synthesized by laterally fusing polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains, suggesting a possible route towards carbon quantum wires.

item.title: Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10966-x Improved molecular insights into inflammatory rheumatic diseases are enabling better disease control and advancing the field towards achieving durable remission and eventual cure.

item.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11214-y An experimental concept enabling attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone is demonstrated and used to visualize the lightwave-driven electron motion of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene.

item.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11181-4 Dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory.

item.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11219-7 In systemic lupus erythematosus, aberrant splicing in neutrophils generates novel peptides that are presented on MHC I, driving CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation, clonal expansion and IgG autoantibody responses, establishing neoantigen-driven autoimmune immunity.

item.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10721-2 Phase 1 of TenK10K takes single-cell RNA sequencing and matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals, enabling detection of associations for common and rare genetic variants, the latter of which have been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1 Sensorimotor and amygdala activation, but not canonical prefrontal control circuits, indicate emotion regulation capacity.

item.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11208-w Tumour assembloids, which model components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts and tumour-infiltrating immune cells, are used to identify an essential pathway that mediates heterogeneous therapeutic responses.

item.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11182-3 In mouse myocardium, glucose oxidation persists in the absence of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, with mitochondrial MCT1 importing lactate into mitochondria and LDHB oxidizing it to pyruvate and NADH, sustaining cardiac energetics and preventing stress-induced heart failure.

item.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11170-7 Cultures reveal conservation of cell structure, physical symbioses and anaerobiosis across Heimdallarchaeia (the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes) and other Promethearchaeota.

item.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11222-y A method for growing infrared image sensors directly from solution using raw materials by monolithic in situ integration of high-performance semiconductor PbS photodetectors on readout integrated circuits is described, yielding films with excellent electronic properties.

item.title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11227-7 Experiments show that altermagnetic Mn5Si3 generates spin currents despite zero net magnetization, demonstrating a central prediction of altermagnetic spintronics.

item.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11147-6 A triplet carbene molecule in a tailored crystal provides a stable single-molecule spin–photon interface with millisecond coherence, advancing chemically engineered molecular qubits for quantum networking.

item.title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11201-3 Experiments show that when subjected to high-frequency stimulation, excitatory neurons exhibit a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity mediated by the exocytosis of v-SNARE protein VAMP7 and the resulting inhibition of P/Q-type calcium channels.

item.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11199-8 Africa-wide water demand analysis across six sectors in 2020 shows that in specific regions of northern and southern Africa, the current water demand exceeds water availability.

item.title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11206-y A multi-ancestry study of Alzheimer’s disease identifies new risk loci and potential drug targets, implicates microglia and neurons, and reveals a larger common-variant contribution than previously estimated.

item.title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11173-4 Single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling identifies cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific genetic effects that link non-coding variants to immune disease risk.

item.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11178-z Pharmacological inhibition of the m7G methyltransferase METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and substantially prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin.

item.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11197-w Loss of function of canonical BAF induces gain of CTCF and cohesin binding that alters 3D genome architecture and reprograms transcription.

item.title: An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur
item.description: Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows Should any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile. Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure . Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door. Continue reading...

item.title: Alexia Putellas a worthy Ballon d’Or winner but the limited shortlist illustrates flaws
item.description: Neglect of African football and a third win for the Spanish great does little to challenge narrative that the prize is reserved only for top nations’ players After a four-year wait, Alexia Putellas is the queen of women’s football once again. Receiving the Ballon d’Or for a record‑equalling third time to continue Spain’s domination of the award, the 32-year-old reinforces her status as one of the greatest players of all time. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga. item.title: The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
item.description: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging.

item.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

item.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
item.description: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

item.title: A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists at UC San Diego have developed a surprising new way to store digital information using light instead of magnets, potentially paving the way for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient memory devices. By precisely shaping and shrinking an ultrafast laser beam, researchers demonstrated that they could switch magnetic states in a material, the basic process used to write digital data. The technique could potentially operate more than 1,000 times faster than conventional magnetic switching methods.

item.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
item.description: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
item.description: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy.

item.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
item.description: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging.

item.title: Sin or virtue? How envy can actually be helpful
item.description: In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals In the 16th-century poem The Faerie Queene, envy is a ghoulish figure riding a ravenous wolf, sad to see the fortune of others and “wonderous glad” of their hardship. It’s not a flattering depiction; better to be thankful for what we have, rather than dwell on such a bitter and self-destructive feeling, right? Maybe not. “I think that when we don’t examine our envy, that’s when it leads us astray,” says Dr Stacy Kim, social scientist, life coach and author of the new book Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want. Kim wrote the book after seeing the way envy came up for her coaching clients and reflecting on the role it had in her own life. item.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Clement was hit by a car and left to die in a ditch – then found his beautiful purpose
item.description: Before being rescued, he had an extremely traumatic experience. You’d never know it though, from the joy his patience and sunny nature bring to those who most need him In December 2024, my kerry blue terrier, Magnus, died suddenly from a stroke at the age of nine. Devastated, I started looking at rescue dogs on Facebook and came across Clement, who was being looked after by a shelter in Romania. It wasn’t his appearance that caught my attention, but his heartbreaking story. An eight-year-old mixed-breed rescue, Clement had spent most of his life with a woman living with Alzheimer’s. One day, she accidentally let him out. He was hit by a car, attacked by two large dogs and left in a ditch for three days in the snow before being rescued by chance. When I read this, I knew I had to take him in. Continue reading...

item.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

item.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
item.description: Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

item.title: Allotmentcore: why everyone is dressing like Barbara in The Good Life
item.description: Clogs, chore jackets, straw hats and woven baskets are the look of the season. But are the brands and people embracing this aesthetic really doing any gardening? Lately, it feels like you can’t move for clogs. Everywhere you look, it’s straw hats, dungarees, floaty dresses, chore jackets and basket bags – and that’s in city centres, not garden centres. item.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
item.description: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

item.title: AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
item.description: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

item.title: Mbappé double secures Real Madrid late victory at Barcelona after Raphinha leveller
item.description: Thirteen years later, José Mourinho led Real Madrid into the Camp Nou as one team and them out again as another having secured the kind of late victory he loves and which opens up a whole new world. With just three minutes and the final reserves of energy remaining, a wonderful moment of skill from Jude Bellingham found Eduardo Camavinga and set them on one last run. Camavinga sprinted free, skilfully slipped Pau Cubarsí and pulled back for Kylian Mbappé to provide the finish, a little bit of history written. “The world that loves football will have stopped to watch this and they won’t have gone disappointed; this was two teams that played to win,” Mourinho said. It had been an intense, breathless ride, a proper battle, and it was his team who won it. Arriving right on time, Mbappé scored his second to make it 2-1, the Camp Nou falling quiet and their team given no time to react. They had drawn level after Mbappé’s opener, Raphinha scoring, but could not do it again. Continue reading..

item.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

item.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

item.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
item.description: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

item.title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots | Philipp Lahm
item.description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward Do we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra. I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri. Continue readi

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
